answers.question: If we double the length and width of a MOSFET, what happens to its intrinsic gain?

answer.text:
The intrinsic gain of a MOSFET is \(A_0=g_mr_o\). In long-channel operation this quantity simplifies to
\[
A_0=\frac{2L}{\lambda'V_{ov}},
\]
where the channel-length modulation parameter has been written \(\lambda=\lambda'/L\).

Doubling both \(W\) and \(L\) leaves the ratio \(W/L\) unchanged. Consequently, when the device is biased at the same gate-source voltage (or, equivalently, at the same drain current), the over-drive \(V_{ov}\) is unchanged while \(L\) itself doubles. The expression above then shows that \(A_0\) exactly doubles.

(The same conclusion is reached by examining the small-signal parameters separately: \(g_m\) is unaltered while \(r_o\) doubles, so their product doubles.)

Final answer: doubles

answers.question: Student A says the transconductance of a MOSFET goes up as the overdrive voltage increases. Student B says it goes down. Who is correct?

answer.text:
The MOSFET saturation transconductance can be written in two equivalent ways:
\[
g_m=\mu C_{\rm ox}\frac{W}{L}V_{\rm OV}=\frac{2I_D}{V_{\rm OV}}.
\]
- With device dimensions held fixed, raising \(V_{\rm OV}\) (i.e., raising \(V_{GS}\)) increases \(g_m\) linearly, so Student A is right.
- With drain current held fixed, raising \(V_{\rm OV}\) requires a smaller \(W/L\) and therefore lowers \(g_m\), so Student B is right.

Both statements are therefore correct once the quantity that is kept constant is specified.

Final answer: both (depends what is fixed)

answers.question: Is the small-signal model of a PMOS device identical to that of an NMOS device?

answer.text:
The small-signal (hybrid-\(\pi\)) model is obtained by linearizing the large-signal device equations about a quiescent bias point. Because only incremental quantities appear, the resulting controlled sources (\(g_m v_{gs}\), \(g_{mb} v_{bs}\)), output resistance, and capacitive elements have identical topology and polarity conventions for both NMOS and PMOS transistors. (All differences in voltage/current sign that exist in the large-signal equations are absorbed into the definitions of the bias point and of the small-signal parameters themselves.)

Final answer: yes

answers.question:
Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 4.

## Figures

![Figure 4](figure-04.png)

answer.text:
The circuit in Figure 4 is an inverting PMOS common-source stage with source degeneration. As drawn, the body is tied to the source, so there is no body effect.

## Topology
- \(M_1\) is a PMOS device. \(V_\mathrm{in}\) drives the gate.
- \(R_S\) sits between the source and \(V_{DD}\) (AC ground), so it is source degeneration.
- \(R_D\) is the drain load to ground, and \(V_\mathrm{out}\) is taken at the drain.

## Bias (saturation)
Let \(I_D>0\) be the bias current magnitude. Then

\[
V_S=V_{DD}-I_D R_S,\qquad V_\mathrm{out}=I_D R_D,\qquad V_{SG}=V_{DD}-I_D R_S-V_\mathrm{in}.
\]

The device is on for \(V_{SG}>|V_{tp}|\). It stays in saturation (the region assumed below) when

\[
V_\mathrm{out}\le V_\mathrm{in}+|V_{tp}|.
\]

With square-law parameters the bias current satisfies

\[
I_D=\frac12\mu_p C_\mathrm{ox}\frac{W}{L}\bigl(V_{DD}-I_D R_S-V_\mathrm{in}-|V_{tp}|\bigr)^2,
\]

which is quadratic in \(I_D\). No numerical values are given, so the operating point stays symbolic. Small-signal parameters at that point are \(g_m\) and \(r_o\approx 1/(\lambda I_D)\).

## Small-signal gain
Midband model: \(V_{DD}\) and ground are AC grounds, gate current is zero, and capacitors are omitted.

Ignoring \(r_o\), KCL at the source and drain gives

\[
A_v=\frac{v_\mathrm{out}}{v_\mathrm{in}}=-\frac{g_m R_D}{1+g_m R_S}.
\]

Including \(r_o\) (body still tied to the source),

\[
A_v=-\frac{g_m R_D}{1+g_m R_S+\dfrac{R_D+R_S}{r_o}}=-\frac{g_m r_o R_D}{r_o+R_D+R_S(1+g_m r_o)}.
\]

Both expressions are negative: raising the gate reduces \(|V_{SG}|\), so \(I_D\) falls and \(V_\mathrm{out}=I_D R_D\) falls. The stage inverts, same as an NMOS common-source stage.

Checks:
- \(R_S=0\) recovers the ordinary common-source gain \(-g_m(R_D\parallel r_o)\).
- \(r_o\to\infty\) recovers \(-g_m R_D/(1+g_m R_S)\).

## Resistances
- \(R_\mathrm{in}=\infty\) at the gate (as drawn; any bias network not shown would set a finite value).
- Resistance looking into the drain, gate AC-grounded:

\[
R_\mathrm{out,device}=r_o+(1+g_m r_o)R_S.
\]

- Resistance at the output node:

\[
R_\mathrm{out}=R_D\parallel\bigl[r_o+(1+g_m r_o)R_S\bigr].
\]

## Role of \(R_S\)
Source degeneration lowers \(|A_v|\) by about \(1+g_m R_S\), raises the resistance seen at the drain by that same factor, and makes the gain much less sensitive to \(g_m\). For strong degeneration (\(g_m R_S\gg 1\) and \(r_o\) large),

\[
A_v\approx -\frac{R_D}{R_S},
\]

set by the resistor ratio rather than by the transistor. The price is lower gain; the benefit is better linearity and bias stability.

answers.question:
Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 5.

## Figures

![Figure 5](figure-05.png)

answer.text:
The circuit is an NMOS source follower (common-drain stage): drain at AC ground (\(V_{DD}\)), input on the gate, output at the source, with \(R_S\) setting the bias current.

### Role of each terminal
- \(V_{DD}\) on the drain is a DC bias only. For small signals the drain is grounded, so this is not a common-source stage.
- \(V_{in}\) drives the gate. DC gate current is zero, so the input resistance is very large (set by leakage or by whatever drives the gate, not by \(M_1\)).
- \(V_{out}\) is the source. \(R_S\) both biases \(M_1\) and is the load the source drives.

### DC bias
With \(M_1\) in saturation,

\[
I_D=\frac12 k_n(V_{GS}-V_t)^2,\qquad V_{out}=I_D R_S,\qquad V_{GS}=V_{in}-V_{out}.
\]

So

\[
V_{out}=\frac12 k_n R_S(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_t)^2.
\]

Solve the quadratic for \(V_{out}\) (the root with \(V_{GS}>V_t\) and \(V_{out}>0\)). Saturation holds when \(V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_t\), i.e. \(V_{DD}\ge V_{in}-V_t\), which is the usual bias region for this stage. Level shift: \(V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{GS}\), with \(V_{GS}\) a few hundred millivolts above \(V_t\).

### Small-signal model
\[
v_{gs}=v_{in}-v_{out}.
\]
The controlled source \(g_m v_{gs}\) (and \(g_{mb} v_{bs}\) if the bulk is not tied to the source) drives the parallel combination of \(R_S\) and \(r_o\).

**Voltage gain** (non-inverting, less than 1):

\[
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_m(R_S\parallel r_o)}{1+(g_m+g_{mb})(R_S\parallel r_o)}.
\]

If the bulk is tied to the source, \(g_{mb}=0\). If \(r_o\gg R_S\) and \(g_m R_S\gg 1\),

\[
A_v\approx\frac{g_m R_S}{1+g_m R_S}\to 1.
\]

Body effect and finite \(r_o\) both pull \(A_v\) further below 1. There is no polarity inversion: the source follows the gate, shifted by \(V_{GS}\).

**Resistances**

- \(R_{in}\to\infty\) at low frequency (gate oxide).
- Looking into the source with the gate AC-grounded,

\[
R_{out}=\frac{1}{g_m+g_{mb}}\parallel R_S\parallel r_o\approx\frac{1}{g_m}\parallel R_S,
\]

which is low when \(g_m\) is large. That low \(R_{out}\) plus near-unity gain is why the stage is used as a buffer.

### What it is not
It does not provide voltage gain greater than 1, and it is a poor choice if you need a precise gain set by a resistor ratio. Swing is limited on the high side by the required \(V_{GS}\) and on the low side by \(M_1\) leaving saturation or by \(I_D R_S\) collapsing as \(V_{in}\) falls toward \(V_t\).

answers.question:
Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 6.

## Figures

![Figure 6](figure-06.png)

answer.text:
The circuit is an NMOS common-gate stage: the gate is the common (AC-grounded) terminal, the signal enters at the source, and the output is taken at the drain.

## Topology

- \(M_1\) is an NMOS (source arrow points into the channel).
- Gate is tied directly to \(V_{DD}\). Since the supply is an AC ground, \(v_g = 0\).
- \(V_{in}\) drives the source, so the source is the input terminal.
- \(V_{out}\) is taken at the drain, with \(R_D\) as the drain load to \(V_{DD}\).

So the gate is common to input and output: this is a common-gate amplifier, not a common-source stage.

## Bias constraint

With the body assumed tied to the source (discrete 3-terminal device, no body effect):

\[
V_{GS} = V_{DD} - V_{in}, \qquad V_{OV} = V_{DD} - V_{in} - V_t
\]

The device is on only for \(V_{in} < V_{DD} - V_t\). Saturation (\(V_{DS} \ge V_{OV}\)) requires

\[
V_{out} \ge V_{DD} - V_t \quad\Rightarrow\quad I_D R_D \le V_t.
\]

Tying the gate all the way to \(V_{DD}\) therefore limits the quiescent drop across \(R_D\) to about one threshold. The small-signal results below assume \(M_1\) is biased in saturation within that constraint.

## Small-signal model

Use \(g_m\) and \(r_o\), gate at AC ground, and \(v_s = v_{in}\), so \(v_{gs} = -v_{in}\).

**Voltage gain.** KCL at the drain gives

\[
A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = \frac{R_D\,(1 + g_m r_o)}{R_D + r_o}.
\]

For \(r_o \gg R_D\),

\[
A_v \approx g_m R_D,
\]

which is positive: the stage is non-inverting. Raising \(v_{in}\) lowers \(V_{GS}\), reduces \(I_D\), and therefore raises \(v_{out}\).

**Input resistance** (looking into the source, drain loaded by \(R_D\)):

\[
R_{in} = \frac{r_o + R_D}{1 + g_m r_o} \approx \frac{1}{g_m}.
\]

The stage has a low input impedance, set by the source, so it wants to be driven by a low-impedance source.

**Output resistance** (input voltage source shorts the source to AC ground):

\[
R_{out} = R_D \parallel r_o \approx R_D.
\]

## Summary

| Property | Result |
|---|---|
| Configuration | Common-gate (source input, drain output, gate at AC ground) |
| Gain | \(+\,R_D(1+g_m r_o)/(R_D+r_o) \approx +g_m R_D\) (non-inverting) |
| \(R_{in}\) | \((r_o+R_D)/(1+g_m r_o) \approx 1/g_m\) (low) |
| \(R_{out}\) | \(R_D \parallel r_o\) (high) |

If this were an integrated device with the body tied to a fixed substrate rather than to the source, replace \(g_m\) by \(g_m + g_{mb}\) in the gain and input-resistance expressions; the conclusions are otherwise unchanged.

It includes valid small-signal derivations and bias constraints, with only minor optional body-effect notes that do not affect the essential result.

answers.question:
Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 9.

## Figures

![Figure 9](figure-09.png)

answer.text:
The circuit is a source-input NMOS stage with series–shunt resistive feedback. It is a non-inverting amplifier whose small-signal gain is set by the loop and, for large loop gain, by the feedback ratio alone.

## Topology

- \(M_1\) is an NMOS. \(V_{in}\) drives the source, the drain is the output, and \(R_D\) is the drain load to \(V_{DD}\).
- \(R_1\)–\(R_2\) sense \(V_{out}\) and return a fraction of it to the gate:
  \[
  V_F=\beta V_{out},\qquad \beta=\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}.
  \]
- The gate current is zero, so that divider equation is exact at DC and at midband.
- Comparison is series mixing at the gate–source port: \(v_{gs}=v_F-v_{in}\). Sampling is voltage sampling at the drain. This is series–shunt (voltage-sampling, series-mixing) negative feedback.

Polarity check: a rise in \(v_{in}\) reduces \(v_{gs}\), reduces \(i_D\), and raises \(v_{out}\). The rise in \(v_{out}\) raises \(v_F\), which restores \(v_{gs}\). The forward gain is positive and the feedback is negative.

## Bias and region of operation

With no gate current,
\[
V_{GS}=V_F-V_{in}=\beta V_{out}-V_{in},
\]
\[
I_D=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_D}=\frac12 k_n(V_{GS}-V_t)^2
\]
in saturation, where \(k_n=\mu_n C_{ox}W/L\). The quiescent point is the solution of that pair for the chosen DC value of \(V_{in}\). Conduction requires \(\beta V_{out}>V_{in}+V_t\), so the allowable DC input level sits well below the output.

The device cannot leave saturation while it is on and \(V_{out}>0\). Because \(V_G=\beta V_{out}<V_{out}\),
\[
V_{GD}=-(1-\beta)V_{out}<0<V_t,
\]
so \(V_{DS}>V_{GS}-V_t\) holds automatically. Triode need not be checked separately.

## Midband small-signal results

Ignore body effect and channel-length modulation for the design equations, then restore \(r_o\). The divider loads the drain with \(R_1+R_2\) and does not load the input. Define
\[
R_L=R_D\parallel(R_1+R_2),\qquad a=g_m R_L,\qquad T=\beta a=\beta g_m R_L.
\]
Nodal analysis (and the series–shunt formulas, which are exact in this unilateral case) gives
\[
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\frac{a}{1+T}=\frac{g_m R_L}{1+\beta g_m R_L},
\]
\[
R_{in}=\frac{1}{g_m}(1+T)=\frac{1}{g_m}+\beta R_L,
\]
\[
R_{out}=\frac{R_L}{1+T}=\frac{R_L}{1+\beta g_m R_L}.
\]
Open-loop reference values are \(A_v\big|_{T=0}=g_m R_L\), \(R_{in}=1/g_m\), and \(R_{out}=R_L\). Feedback therefore lowers the gain, raises the resistance seen by the source driving \(V_{in}\), and lowers the output resistance, all by \(1+T\).

If loop gain is large, \(v_{gs}\to 0\) incrementally, so \(v_F\approx v_{in}\) and
\[
A_v\to\frac{1}{\beta}=1+\frac{R_1}{R_2}.
\]
The closed-loop gain is then set by the resistor ratio, in the same way as an op-amp non-inverting stage. The DC \(V_{GS}\) remains large; only the incremental gate–source voltage is suppressed. Linearity improves as \(T\) increases because the square-law device is enclosed by the loop.

With finite \(r_o\), \(r_o\) ties source to drain, so the stage is no longer unilateral and the simple \(1+T\) split is only approximate. The exact midband results are
\[
A_v=\frac{g_m+1/r_o}{1/R_L+\beta g_m+1/r_o},\qquad
R_{out}=\frac{1}{1/R_L+\beta g_m+1/r_o},
\]
\[
R_{in}=\frac{1/R_L+\beta g_m+1/r_o}{(1/R_L)\,(g_m+1/r_o)}.
\]
They reduce to the expressions above as \(r_o\to\infty\).

## Body effect and frequency

If the bulk is tied to the source, there is no body effect and the results stand. If the bulk is grounded while the source carries the signal, a \(g_{mb}v_{bs}\) term appears. It adds to the input transconductance but not to the gate feedback term \(\beta g_m\), so \(g_m\) cannot simply be replaced by \(g_m+g_{mb}\) everywhere; \(R_{in}\) falls and the gain expression changes.

At high frequency the same topology applies with \(C_{gs}\), \(C_{gd}\), and \(C_{db}\) (and \(C_{sb}\) if the bulk is AC-grounded) included. \(C_{gd}\) and the feedback network set the dominant output pole; the series–shunt loop still desensitizes the midband gain, but the loop gain falls once those capacitances conduct.

**Large-signal behavior.**  
With \(V_b\) fixed, \(M_2\) (saturation) sets the bias current
\[
I_D=\frac12\mu_nC_{ox}\Bigl(\frac WL\Bigr)_2(V_b-V_t)^2
\]
(neglecting channel-length modulation). The same current flows in \(M_1\), forcing
\[
V_{GS1}=V_t+\sqrt{\frac{2I_D}{\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1}},

so
\[

\]
Thus the stage performs a DC level shift while the signal component of \(V_{out}\) follows \(V_{in}\). Both devices remain in saturation only for
\[

The circuit is a source follower driving a common-gate stage (equivalently, a single-ended-input, single-ended-output differential pair).

## Topology

Both devices are NMOS. The tail source \(I_1\) is an ideal DC current (AC open).

- **\(M_1\)** — drain at AC ground (\(V_{DD}\)), input on the gate, source as the output: **source follower** (common-drain).
- **\(M_2\)** — gate at AC ground (\(V_b\) is bias only), input on the source, drain as the output with load \(R_D\): **common-gate**.
- The follower’s source drives the common-gate source directly. With a shared tail current this is exactly a differential pair: \(v_{in}\) is a single-ended input, \(V_b\) is the reference gate, and \(v_{out}\) is taken from only one drain.

## DC bias

\[
I_1 = I_{D1} + I_{D2}, \qquad V_X = V_{in} - V_{GS1} = V_b - V_{GS2}.
\]

If \(V_{in}=V_b\) (DC) and the devices are matched, \(I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1/2\) and

\[
V_{OUT} = V_{DD} - \frac{I_1}{2}R_D.
\]

Both transistors must stay in saturation: \(V_{DD}-V_X > V_{ov1}\) and \(V_{OUT}-V_X \ge V_{ov2}\).

## Small-signal gain

Bodies sit at the same \(V_{SB}\), so \(\eta=g_{mb}/g_m\) is the same for both devices. With \(r_o\to\infty\), KCL at the source node (tail is an AC open, so \(i_{d1}=-i_{d2}\)) gives

\[
\frac{v_x}{v_{in}} = \frac{g_{m1}}{(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(1+\eta)}, \qquad \frac{v_{out}}{v_x} = g_{m2}(1+\eta)R_D.
\]

The body-effect factors cancel, leaving

\[
A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = \frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D = (g_{m1}\parallel g_{m2})\,R_D.
\]

For a matched pair (\(g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m\))

\[
A_v = \frac{g_m R_D}{2}.
\]

The gain is **non-inverting**: \(v_{in}\uparrow\) raises \(v_x\), which reduces \(V_{GS2}\), steers current away from \(R_D\), and raises \(v_{out}\). This is the same result as the differential-pair formula \(v_{out}/v_{id}=g_m R_D/2\) with \(v_{id}=v_{in}\) (other gate AC-grounded) and an ideal tail (common-mode gain is zero).

**Stage view (why the title fits):** the follower is loaded by the common-gate input resistance \(1/[g_{m2}(1+\eta)]\). Its loaded gain times the common-gate gain \((g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_D\) again yields \((g_{m1}\parallel g_{m2})R_D\).

### Channel-length modulation

With finite \(r_o\) and matched devices the same calculation gives

\[
A_v = \frac{g_m}{2}\,(R_D \parallel 2r_o).
\]

So the ideal factor \(g_m/2\) is unchanged; the load is just degenerated by the resistance seen looking into \(M_2\)’s drain (\(\approx 2r_o\)).

Unmatched, with \(G_1=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+1/r_{o1}\) and \(G_2=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+1/r_{o2}\),

\[
A_v = \frac{g_{m1}\,G_2\,R_D\,r_{o2}}{G_1(R_D+r_{o2})+G_2\,r_{o2}}.
\]

## Impedances

- **Input:** gate of \(M_1\), so \(R_{in}=\infty\).
- **Output, excluding \(R_D\):** the source of \(M_2\) is terminated by the follower’s source resistance \(1/G_1\), so

\[
R_o = r_{o2}\!\left(1+\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}{G_1}\right)+\frac{1}{G_1}.
\]

Matched and \(g_m r_o\gg 1\): \(R_o\approx 2r_o\). The resistance that actually loads the gain is \(R_o\parallel R_D\), which is what produced \(R_D\parallel 2r_o\) above.

## Design remarks

- Maximum \((g_{m1}\parallel g_{m2})\) for a fixed tail is the matched bias \(g_m/2\), so \(|A_v|\) cannot exceed \(g_m R_D/2\). A common-source stage using the full tail current has a larger \(|g_m R_D|\), but it inverts and does not provide the differential-pair’s supply/common-mode rejection.
- Body effect does **not** reduce \(A_v\): both devices share \(V_{SB}\), so \(\eta\) raises the follower’s source conductance and the common-gate transconductance by the same factor and cancels.
- Useful signal swing at the output is set by keeping \(M_2\) saturated: \(V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_D-V_X\ge V_{ov2}\), while \(V_X\) itself must leave enough \(V_{DS}\) on the tail device.

## Figures

![Figure 23](figure-23.png)

answer.text:
The circuit in Figure 23 is a shunt–shunt feedback transimpedance amplifier (TIA): it converts the signal current \(I_{\mathrm{in}}\) into the voltage \(V_{\mathrm{out}}\).

## Topology

- **\(M_1\)** is an NMOS common-gate stage. Its gate is AC-grounded by the bias \(V_b\), its source is the input node, and its drain is the intermediate node \(X\), loaded by \(R_{D1}\).
- **\(M_2\)** is an NMOS common-source stage. Its gate is driven by \(X\), its source is grounded, and its drain is the output, loaded by \(R_{D2}\).
- **\(R_F\)** closes a feedback loop from \(V_{\mathrm{out}}\) back to the input node. The indicated \(i_{RF}\) is the feedback current.

Sampling is of output voltage (shunt at the output); mixing is of input current (shunt at the input). That is the shunt–shunt topology, whose ideal closed-loop parameter is a transimpedance.

## Feedback sign

Raising \(I_{\mathrm{in}}\) raises the source of \(M_1\), so \(V_{GS1}\) and \(I_{D1}\) fall and \(V_X\) rises. \(M_2\) then conducts more and \(V_{\mathrm{out}}\) falls. The lower \(V_{\mathrm{out}}\) pulls current out of the input node through \(R_F\), opposing \(I_{\mathrm{in}}\). The feedback is negative, and the gain \(V_{\mathrm{out}}/I_{\mathrm{in}}\) is negative.

## Small-signal model

Use
\[
g_{m1}'=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}
\]
for \(M_1\) (source is not at the body). \(M_2\) has no body effect if its body is tied to its source. Take \(r_{o1}\to\infty\) (the usual CG simplification; finite \(r_{o1}\) is noted below), keep \(r_{o2}\), and neglect gate current. Direct feedthrough through \(R_F\) is negligible next to the amplified path when the two-stage voltage gain is large.

## Open-loop amplifier and feedback factor

For shunt–shunt feedback the feedback network is represented by \(y\)-parameters. With port voltages defined into the network,
\[
y_{11f}=y_{22f}=\frac{1}{R_F},\qquad y_{12f}=y_{21f}=-\frac{1}{R_F}.
\]
The feedback factor and the ideal closed-loop gain are
\[
\beta=y_{12f}=-\frac{1}{R_F},\qquad \frac{1}{\beta}=-R_F.
\]

In the \(A\)-circuit the controlled source of the feedback network is removed and the loading \(y_{11f}\), \(y_{22f}\) is retained, so \(R_F\) appears from the input node to ground and from the output node to ground.

- Input resistance of \(M_1\) alone: \(R_{\mathrm{in},M1}=1/g_{m1}'\).
- With feedback loading: \(R_{\mathrm{in},A}=R_F\parallel(1/g_{m1}')\).
- Voltage at \(X\): essentially all of the current that enters the source of \(M_1\) flows in \(R_{D1}\), and \(V_X/V_i=g_{m1}'R_{D1}\).
- Output load: \(R_{L2}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_F\), so \(V_{\mathrm{out}}/V_X=-g_{m2}R_{L2}\).

The open-loop transimpedance is therefore
\[
A=\frac{V_{\mathrm{out}}}{I_{\mathrm{in}}}\Big|_{A}
=-\frac{g_{m1}'R_F}{1+g_{m1}'R_F}\,R_{D1}\,g_{m2}R_{L2}.
\]
(\(A<0\), as required.)

## Loop gain and closed-loop transimpedance

\[
L=A\beta=\frac{g_{m1}'R_{D1}\,g_{m2}R_{L2}}{1+g_{m1}'R_F}>0.
\]
Black’s formula gives
\[
\frac{V_{\mathrm{out}}}{I_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{A}{1+L}
=-R_F\cdot\frac{g_{m1}'R_{D1}\,g_{m2}R_{L2}}{1+g_{m1}'R_F+g_{m1}'R_{D1}\,g_{m2}R_{L2}}.
\]
If the loop gain is large,
\[
g_{m1}'R_{D1}\,g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_F)\gg 1+g_{m1}'R_F,
\]
this collapses to the design equation of the TIA:
\[
\frac{V_{\mathrm{out}}}{I_{\mathrm{in}}}\approx -R_F.
\]
The gain is set by a resistor, and device-parameter variation is desensitized by \(1+L\).

## Closed-loop port resistances

Shunt mixing and shunt sampling both divide the corresponding open-loop resistance by \(1+L\):

\[
R_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{R_{\mathrm{in},A}}{1+L}
=\frac{R_F}{1+g_{m1}'R_F+g_{m1}'R_{D1}\,g_{m2}R_{L2}}
\approx\frac{1+g_{m1}'R_F}{g_{m1}'R_{D1}\,g_{m2}}
\cdot\frac{R_F}{R_{L2}(1+g_{m1}'R_F)}
\]
and, for large \(L\),
\[
R_{\mathrm{in}}\approx\frac{R_F}{g_{m1}'R_{D1}\,g_{m2}R_{L2}}\ll\frac{1}{g_{m1}'}.
\]
The low input resistance is what a current-input amplifier wants: most of \(I_{\mathrm{in}}\) enters the amplifier rather than being lost in the source impedance.

\[
R_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{R_{L2}}{1+L}
\approx\frac{1+g_{m1}'R_F}{g_{m1}'R_{D1}\,g_{m2}}.
\]
The low output resistance is appropriate for a voltage output.

## Finite \(r_{o1}\)

If channel-length modulation of \(M_1\) is kept, the CG source resistance becomes
\[
R_{\mathrm{in},M1}=\frac{R_{D1}+r_{o1}}{1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}}
\]
instead of \(1/g_{m1}'\), and only the fraction \(r_{o1}/(r_{o1}+R_{D1})\) of the source current reaches \(R_{D1}\). For \(r_{o1}\gg R_{D1}\) and \(g_{m1}'r_{o1}\gg 1\) both corrections vanish and the results above are recovered. \(r_{o2}\) is already included in \(R_{L2}\).

## What the topology is doing

| Quantity | Open loop (\(A\)-circuit) | Closed loop, \(L\gg 1\) |
|---|---|---|
| Transimpedance | \(A= -\dfrac{g_{m1}'R_F}{1+g_{m1}'R_F}R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{L2}\) | \(\approx -R_F\) |
| \(R_{\mathrm{in}}\) | \(R_F\parallel 1/g_{m1}'\) | \(\approx R_F/(g_{m1}'R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{L2})\) |
| \(R_{\mathrm{out}}\) | \(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_F\) | \(\approx(1+g_{m1}'R_F)/(g_{m1}'R_{D1}g_{m2})\) |

- \(M_1\) already presents a low resistance \(1/g_{m1}'\) and has no Miller multiplication of \(C_{gd1}\) (gate is AC-grounded), which is why a common-gate device is a natural TIA front end.
- \(M_2\) supplies the voltage gain that makes \(L\) large, so the closed-loop gain can sit at \(-R_F\) rather than at the poorly controlled open-loop value.
- The price of two gain stages inside the loop is two high-impedance poles (node \(X\), especially, because of Miller \(C_{gd2}\), and the output node). Feedback widens the closed-loop bandwidth by about \(1+L\), but pole splitting / phase margin has to be checked; the schematic shows no explicit compensation capacitor.

**DC note.** With \(I_{\mathrm{in}}\) a pure signal, the bias current of \(M_1\) must close through \(R_F\), so \(V_{\mathrm{out}}-V_{S1}=I_{D1}R_F\) at the bias point. \(V_b\) sets \(I_{D1}\) and \(V_{S1}\); the output bias point must remain high enough for \(M_2\) to stay in saturation.

\[
W_{\mathrm{eq}}=W,\qquad L_{\mathrm{eq}}=2L,\qquad V_{GS}=V_{\mathrm{in}}.
\]

**Triode region of the composite** (\(V_{\mathrm{out}}<V_{OV}\)). Both devices are in triode:

\[
\frac{I_D}{K_P}=V_{OV}V_x-\frac{V_x^2}{2}
=\bigl(V_{OV}-V_x\bigr)\bigl(V_{\mathrm{out}}-V_x\bigr)-\frac{(V_{\mathrm{out}}-V_x)^2}{2}.
\]

Adding these two expressions cancels every \(V_x\) term and leaves

\[
I_D=\mu_n C_{\mathrm{ox}}\frac{W}{2L}\left[(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_t)V_{\mathrm{out}}-\frac{V_{\mathrm{out}}^2}{2}\right],
\]

which is the triode law of a device of length \(2L\).

**Saturation region of the composite.** \(M_1\) is in triode and \(M_2\) is saturated. Solving the two current equations gives the physical root

\[
V_x=\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_t),\qquad V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_x-V_t=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_t}{\sqrt{2}}.
\]

Substitution then yields

\[
I_D=\frac12\mu_n C_{\mathrm{ox}}\frac{W}{2L}(V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_t)^2.
\]

- \(V_{\mathrm{in}}<V_t\): both devices off, \(I_D=0\), \(V_{\mathrm{out}}=V_{DD}\).
- \(V_{\mathrm{in}}>V_t\) and \(V_{\mathrm{out}}\ge V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_t\): composite in saturation, so \(I_D\) is the \(L_{\mathrm{eq}}=2L\) square law above.
- \(V_{\mathrm{out}}<V_{\mathrm{in}}-V_t\): composite in triode, and \(V_{\mathrm{out}}\) is set by the triode equation together with the load line.

At a given \(V_{OV}\), the stack draws half the current of a single device of length \(L\).

At a saturation bias point the equivalent transistor has

\[

\[

\[
V_{t2}=V_{t0}+\gamma\left(\sqrt{V_x+2\phi_F}-\sqrt{2\phi_F}\right)>V_{t1},
\]

\[

=
\frac{R_{D2}\bigl(1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_F\bigr)}
{1+g_{m1}R_F+g_{m1}R_{D2}+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}.
\]

The same result falls out of the return ratio evaluated by breaking the loop at the gate of \(M_2\) (a unilateral point):

\[
T=\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{1+g_{m1}(R_F+R_{D2})},
\qquad
A_\infty=-R_F,
\qquad
A_d=\frac{R_{D2}}{1+g_{m1}(R_F+R_{D2})},
\]

\[
\frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}=\frac{A_\infty T+A_d}{1+T}.
\]

\(A_\infty=-R_F\) is the gain as \(T\to\infty\). \(A_d\) is the direct feedthrough through \(R_F\) with the controlled source of \(M_2\) killed. Feedthrough is negligible in any useful design:

\[
\frac{A_d}{R_F T}=\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_F}\ll 1,
\]

\[
\frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}\approx -R_F\frac{T}{1+T}\approx -R_F
\quad\text{for }T\gg 1.
\]

\[
T\approx g_{m2}R_{D2}\cdot\frac{R_{D1}}{R_F}.
\]

\[
Z_{in,OL}=\frac{1}{g_{m1}}\parallel(R_F+R_{D2}),
\qquad
Z_{out,OL}=R_{D2}\parallel\Bigl(R_F+\frac{1}{g_{m1}}\Bigr).
\]

\[
Z_{in}=\frac{Z_{in,OL}}{1+T}
=\frac{R_F+R_{D2}}{1+g_{m1}R_F+g_{m1}R_{D2}+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}},
\]

\[
Z_{out}=\frac{Z_{out,OL}}{1+T}
=\frac{R_{D2}(1+g_{m1}R_F)}{1+g_{m1}R_F+g_{m1}R_{D2}+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}.
\]

\[

\qquad
Z_{out}\approx\frac{R_F}{g_{m2}R_{D1}}.
\]

The dominant input-referred current noise of the feedback element is \(4kT/R_F\). Raising \(R_F\) therefore improves both gain and noise, but, from the expression for \(T\), it also reduces loop gain and makes the input pole more troublesome. Finite \(r_o\) lowers the forward gain (and thus \(T\)) and adds a feedforward path from the source of \(M_1\) to \(X\); the ideal gain remains \(-R_F\), but the error terms above get worse.

\[
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_m}{g_m+g_{mb}+1/R_S+1/r_o}.
\]

If \(r_o\to\infty\),

\[
A_v=\frac{g_m R_S}{1+(g_m+g_{mb})R_S}.
\]

- **\(R_F\)** closes a shunt–shunt loop: it samples \(V_\mathrm{out}\) and returns a current to the input node. The overall open-loop path (noninverting CG followed by inverting CS) is inverting, so the feedback is negative.

The quantity stabilized by this feedback is the transimpedance \(V_\mathrm{out}/I_\mathrm{in}\).

## Closed-loop gain

With high loop gain the input node is a virtual ground and essentially all of \(I_\mathrm{in}\) is steered through \(R_F\):

\[
\frac{V_\mathrm{out}}{I_\mathrm{in}} \approx -R_F
\]

The small residual error current, not \(I_\mathrm{in}\) itself, is what enters the source of \(M_1\) and is amplified.

## Midband small-signal result

Neglecting \(r_o\) and body effect, KCL at the source node, node \(X\), and the output gives the exact transimpedance

\[
\frac{V_\mathrm{out}}{I_\mathrm{in}}
= -R_F\,
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}-R_{D2}/R_F}
{1+g_{m1}(R_F+R_{D2})+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}.
\]

The term \(R_{D2}/R_F\) is feedforward through \(R_F\). When the loop gain is large it is negligible and the expression collapses to \(-R_F\).

Two practical corrections:

- Body effect in \(M_1\) (source not at the body) replaces \(g_{m1}\) by \(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}\).
- Channel-length modulation puts \(r_{o2}\) in parallel with \(R_{D2}\); \(r_{o1}\) also shunts the CG stage.

Breaking the loop while retaining the loading of \(R_F\) ( \(R_F\) to ground at the input port, \(R_F\) in parallel with \(R_{D2}\) at the output) yields

\[
A_\mathrm{ol}
= -\frac{g_{m1}R_F}{1+g_{m1}R_F}\,g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\parallel R_F),
\qquad
\beta=-\frac{1}{R_F},
\]

\[
L=A_\mathrm{ol}\beta
= \frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}R_F}{(1+g_{m1}R_F)(R_{D2}+R_F)}.
\]

If \(g_{m1}R_F\gg 1\) and \(R_F\gg R_{D2}\),

\[
L\approx \frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{R_F}.
\]

So \(L\gg 1\) only when the open-loop transimpedance \(g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\) is much larger than the desired closed-loop value \(R_F\). Under that condition

\[
\frac{V_\mathrm{out}}{I_\mathrm{in}}=-R_F\frac{L}{1+L}\approx -R_F.
\]

Shunt–shunt feedback lowers both port impedances by \(1+L\):

\[
R_\mathrm{in}\approx\frac{1/g_{m1}}{1+L},
\qquad
R_\mathrm{out}\approx\frac{R_{D2}\parallel R_F}{1+L}.
\]

The CG device already makes \(R_\mathrm{in}\) small; the loop makes it smaller still, which is what a current-input stage needs.

If \(I_\mathrm{in}\) has no DC component, the bias current of \(M_1\) has nowhere to go except through \(R_F\), so

\[
V_S=V_\mathrm{out}+I_{D1}R_F, \qquad V_X=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1}=V_{GS2},
\]

and KCL at the output is \((V_{DD}-V_\mathrm{out})/R_{D2}+I_{D1}=I_{D2}\). \(V_b\) is chosen so both MOSFETs stay in saturation (\(V_X>V_b-V_{TH1}\) and \(V_\mathrm{out}>V_X-V_{TH2}\)). The large \(I_{D1}R_F\) drop is the main bias constraint on how large \(R_F\) may be.

- Closed-loop gain is set by \(R_F\), not by the poorly controlled \(g_m R_D\) products, provided \(L\gg 1\).
- Accuracy, desensitivity, and the very low \(R_\mathrm{in}\) all improve as \(g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}/R_F\) is increased — but a larger \(R_F\) directly reduces \(L\), so gain and loop gain must be traded.

If the LDO regulator in Figure 15 generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

## Figures

![Figure 15](figure-15.png)

The LDO output noise voltage appears as a common-mode disturbance on the oscillator supply. Because the tank capacitance (varactors plus device parasitics) is voltage-dependent, this disturbance modulates the oscillation frequency. With the one-sided supply-pushing factor defined by
\[
K_{VDD}=\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{\rm out}},
\]
the spectrum of the resulting frequency fluctuations is simply \(K_{VDD}^2S_{\rm th}\). Conversion from frequency noise to phase noise then supplies the single-sideband phase-noise density
\[
\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)=\frac{K_{VDD}^2S_{\rm th}(\Delta f)}{2(\Delta f)^2}.
\]
(The same relation is obtained by writing the excess phase as the integral of the instantaneous frequency deviation and converting the resulting power spectral density into the standard IEEE definition of \(\mathcal{L}\).) For any practical LDO the noise spectrum \(S_{\rm th}\) is confined to low frequencies, so additive contributions that would arise from noise components lying near the carrier itself may be neglected.

Final answer: \(\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)=K_{VDD}^{2}S_{th}/[2(\Delta f)^{2}]\)
